title: The Index Before the Answer
description: Nine tools that work on retrieval and context before generation: compiler call graphs, local indexes, AST pruning, tool catalogs and provenance-aware selection.

images.alt: Lines of code on a monitor with a search panel open
images.caption: Before a model can answer well, something has to decide what reaches its context window.

content:
# The Index Before the Answer

Most arguments about agent quality are arguments about the model. The nine tools here are about the step before the model is called: what gets retrieved, what gets indexed, what gets pruned, and what gets carried from one session into the next. It is unglamorous work, but it is where a lot of the token bill and a lot of the wrong answers originate. Several of these projects share the same quiet claim, that a better index beats a bigger context window, and they approach it from compiler infrastructure, local search, graph inference and plain team convention.

## Answers from the compiler, not from grep

[[link:/tools/2310|Lantern Lattice]] is the most principled of the group. It builds a call graph from your compiler or type checker and exposes it as tools for humans and coding agents, so a get on a specific object resolves to the get of that object's type rather than every get in the repository. Commands trace who calls a symbol, show what uncommitted changes touch and what depends on them, search symbols by regular expression, and grep text while naming the symbol it sits in. It also provides agent-facing replacements for Grep, Glob, Read, Edit and Write so the graph stays current as the agent works. Rust, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, C and C++ are supported, each through its own language tooling, which is also the catch: exact answers require the corresponding language servers to be installed, and the binaries are unsigned.

[[link:/tools/2311|Readfirst]] solves a different retrieval problem, the knowledge that is not in the code at all. It keeps team knowledge in a map file next to the code and hands it out file by file at the moment someone is about to change something: amounts here are in cents, this table is read by the mobile app, run the payment end-to-end test after touching this. A read command returns rules, risks, checks, tests and callers; a verify command confirms the checks pass and that nothing tied to the change was skipped. There is no server, no account and no model call, and it is MIT licensed. It can also scan a repository without a map for fixed bug shapes, such as a computed result that is thrown away or an assertion that never runs because nobody awaited it. It needs Node 20 or newer and, realistically, a team willing to commit and maintain the map.

[[link:/tools/2312|Sweet-search]] challenges the reflex that a coding agent should reach for grep and Read. It offers six purpose-built tools, search, grep, find, semantic, trace and read, behind an index you build once and which updates itself as you edit, including uncommitted changes. It is entirely local with no API keys, no cloud and no Docker, and it wires into Claude Code, Codex and opencode. The project reports cheaper agent runs across 200 real engineering tasks with the same solve count and faster retrieval than classic grep-and-read. It requires Node 22 or newer and downloads models into a local cache at setup, which is the price of keeping the code on your machine.

## Cutting the context down

[[link:/tools/2313|Ctxfw]] operates at the syntax tree layer. It is an in-memory Tree-Sitter AST context firewall and pruning MCP server that replaces distance-one and distance-two-plus module implementations with clean interface signatures, type definitions and functional stubs, reporting substantially less token mass in its own benchmarks. It also runs a deterministic intake sieve that rejects architecture briefs missing negative invariants, bounded variable domains or formal error taxonomies, and it claims zero network telemetry in standard operating mode. It is open-core, with separately priced source capsules listed in the README, and the published numbers are the project's own internal measurements rather than an independent evaluation.

[[link:/tools/2314|MCP ToolSearch Proxy]] addresses a related but often overlooked cost, the tool definitions themselves. Instead of listing hundreds or thousands of MCP tools to a model, it puts five tools in front of the catalog: find tools by description with schemas of the best few, describe up to ten in full, call a read-only tool, batch read-only calls, and call any tool including writes. A call whose arguments do not fit the input schema is refused before it reaches the upstream server, with the schema and the error so the model can fix it at once. Reads and writes are separate tools so clients can allow the first without prompting and keep asking on every write; writes are never batched. The proxy holds no credentials and forwards only the caller's Authorization header. One caveat for operators: tools the upstream has not marked read-only are treated as writes.

[[link:/tools/2316|Thinker]] looks at the same bill from the session side. Its illustrated walkthrough shows how one task triggers many model calls, each carrying earlier context again, and how cached reads still cost money across a long session. It offers three levers: context compression that removes older tool results after use while keeping recent context, instruction analysis that finds guidance worth trimming in files like AGENTS.md for you to review and approve, and a knowledge cache that saves a long exploration as a short reusable note. It connects through the settings of agents you already use. The numbers on the site are explicitly an illustrative example, and compression is automatic only where the host agent supports it.

[[link:/tools/2315|Omneum]] is the most theoretical of the group and the most interesting on provenance. It is an open-source context control plane that evaluates structured observations without reading source text strings or invoking an LLM judge. It iteratively computes source reliability and claim support across a bipartite graph, accounting for the fact that five reports from different sources may all derive from one upstream source, then reconstructs context by selecting original retrieved passages for relevance and incremental claim coverage under a token budget. Observations persist across sessions in a Context Graph backed by SQLite or PostgreSQL. A shipped demo compares naive retrieval-order packing with claim-coverage selection on five chunks, four claims and an 80-unit budget. That is a small demonstration, and adopting it means modelling your context as observations and claims.

## Memory that outlives one app

[[link:/tools/2317|Memex]] starts from the observation that your repo remembers the code but not you. It is an open-source context layer you own, an MCP server running on your own Supabase project where durable facts such as preferences, decisions, corrections and stable project background are kept in your own database and read by any agent. One agent pushes what it knows worth keeping and another pulls it without duplicates; search blends meaning with exact words, favors recent notes and shows the current version of anything that was corrected. A pull-only mode fetches without saving, so nothing needs approval, and you decide per agent what it may save. Code-specific context stays in the repo's CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, and agents are told to leave it out. The site labels it a work in progress, and setup has an agent create tables and deploy a server with your approval at each step.

[[link:/tools/2318|Wenlan]] turns notes, code and earlier AI chats into a living wiki that is checked against sources. Its defining behaviour is refusal: a page is rejected when most of its citations do not match the source, and each citation opens the original. When a source, page or code line changes, only the pages that rely on it are flagged. Notes stay on your machine as local Markdown and go only to the AI tools you pick, and the app never edits existing notes without your approval. It connects to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI and others through MCP, plugins or skills. It uses the AI tool you already have rather than bundling a model, and the desktop app currently targets macOS 11 or later on Apple Silicon or Windows x64.

## The shared bet

Every one of these tools assumes the context window is a budget to be spent deliberately, not a bucket to be filled. Some spend it on compiler-resolved symbols, some on local semantic indexes, some on interface stubs, and some on durable facts about the person doing the work. A few of them also assume you will keep that budget on hardware you own, which is a notable pattern across this batch. The risk is setup complexity and a layer of indirection between the agent and the raw files, and the projects that publish their own benchmarks are careful to say the numbers are theirs. But the direction is consistent: retrieval is becoming a designed subsystem rather than a single grep call.
tldr: Lantern Lattice, Readfirst, Sweet-search, Ctxfw, MCP ToolSearch Proxy, Omneum, Thinker, Memex and Wenlan all decide what enters a context window.
